did_you_know.text: The phrase “a land flowing with milk and honey” describes a land of abundance. In the Bible, the word “honey” may also refer to sweet date syrup, not only to bee honey.
The first word, “Shema,” is a command meaning to listen and take something to heart, not merely to hear sounds. This verse became Judaism’s central declaration of faith.
In the Bible, “heart” often refers to the center of thought and will, not only to emotion. In rabbinic tradition, “with all your might” can also mean giving all your resources and ability.
The verb “veshinantam” is related to the word “tooth” and the idea of sharpening. The verse suggests that learning becomes clear and precise through repetition and regular conversation.
The Sages interpreted this verse as a command to wear tefillin on the arm and head. The word “totafot” is rare in the Bible, and its exact meaning is uncertain.
The word “mezuzah” originally means a doorpost or part of a doorway; later it also became the name of the parchment placed there. The parchment contains the passages “Shema” and “Vehayah im shamoa.”
Rock-cut cisterns were used to store rainwater, especially important in a land with dry summers. A water cistern was therefore a major asset in ancient settlements.
The name “Massah” is connected with the Hebrew root meaning “to test” or “to try.” According to Exodus, the place received this name after the people quarreled over the lack of water and tested God.
